To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
leaf area distribution was influenced more by stem density, whereas total leaf area, dry matter production, and growth rate were influenced more by plant density.
stem density does not affect potato canopy development and production in the field.
the growth and development of basal lateral branches in 1S potato canopies offset any initial advantage of multiple-stemmed potato plants in leaf area production.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of stem number on potato growth and development.
understanding the effect of stem density on potato canopy development, growth, and dry matter partitioning.

the development of a potato model that can be used to predict the growth and development of the potato canopy under various environmental conditions and to predict the yield and quality of the potato crop.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the differences in canopy development and growth between single- and triple-stemmed potato are small enough to not be a concern for modeling or research purposes.
the differences between single- and multi-stemmed plants in controlled environment studies are small and can be ignored.
, in general, single- versus multiple-stemmed potato plant responses on a per plant basis can be extrapolated, with some exceptions, to the field where potato plants are commonly multi-stemmed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

single-stemmed potato plants are a reasonable proxy for multiple-stemmed potato in growth chamber experiments, but that researchers must be cognizant of the potential for differences in canopy structure, particularly in leaf area distribution, between single- and multi-stemmed plants.
, given adequate nutrition, the number of potato stems per plant does not affect canopy leaf area, dry matter production, or tuber yield on a per unit area basis.
single-stemmed potato plants are a valid model for field-grown plants, but only if the plants are late maturing and adequately supplied with nutrients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for a given stem density, the leaf area distribution of the potato canopy is different than that of a single-stemmed plant.
researchers should not assume that responses from single-stemed potato plants can be extended directly to the field where multi-stemed plants are common.
single- and multiple- stem densities can have a significant effect on the leaf area distribution of potato plants and, therefore, on the light interception and photosynthetic potential of the canopy.
